question_text: For which real \(t\) is the angle between \((t,1)\) and \((2,-3)\) obtuse (strictly between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\))?
worked_solution: \(\cos\theta\) has the sign of \((t,1)\cdot(2,-3)=2t-3\). The angle is obtuse when \(-1<\cos\theta<0\). \(2t-3<0\) gives \(t<\tfrac32\). \(\cos\theta=-1\) happens when \((t,1)\) is a negative multiple of \((2,-3)\): \((t,1)=-\tfrac13(2,-3)\), i.e. \(t=-\tfrac23\). So \(t<\tfrac32\), \(t\ne-\tfrac23\).

question_text: \(X\sim B(n,p)\) and \(Y\sim B(m,q)\) are independent. Which statement about \(X+Y\) is correct?

correct_answer: \(X+Y\sim B(n+m,p)\) when \(q=p\); otherwise it need not be binomial.
worked_solution: With a common \(p\), think of \(n\) trials followed by \(m\) more, all independent with success probability \(p\): the total count is \(B(n+m,p)\). question_text: For an arbitrary data set (any shape) with population standard deviation \(\sigma>0\), what is the largest proportion that is guaranteed to lie strictly within \(2\sigma\) of the mean?

question_text: On an Argand diagram, what is the locus of points \(z\) with \(\arg(z-2)=\dfrac\pi4\)?

question_text: Let \(p\) be a polynomial with real coefficients and \(p(z)=0\). Which argument proves that \(p(\bar z)=0\)?
options: [{"option_id":"A","text":"Because \\(p(-z)=-p(z)\\) for every real polynomial."},{"option_id":"B","text":"Because every root satisfies \\(\\bar z=-z\\), so \\(p(\\bar z)=p(-z)=0\\)."},{"option_id":"C","text":"Because \\(p(z)=0\\) forces \\(z\\) to be real, so \\(\\bar z=z\\)."},{"option_id":"D","text":"Because the coefficients are real, \\(p(\\bar z)=\\overline{p(z)}=\\overline0=0\\)."}]
correct_answer: Because the coefficients are real, \(p(\bar z)=\overline{p(z)}=\overline0=0\).
worked_solution: For real \(a_k\): \(\overline{p(z)}=\sum\overline{a_k}\,\bar z^k=\sum a_k\bar z^k=p(\bar z)\). The identity \(p(\bar z)=\overline{p(z)}\) was verified symbolically for a general real cubic with \(z=a+bi\); the same computation works term by term for any degree. The other options are refuted by the counterexamples shown.

question_text: Which argument correctly identifies the locus \(|z|=2|z-3|\) on an Argand diagram?
options: [{"option_id":"A","text":"It is the perpendicular bisector \\(x=\\tfrac32\\) of \\(0\\) and \\(3\\), since distances are compared."},{"option_id":"B","text":"It is the circle with centre \\((3,0)\\) and radius \\(2\\)."},{"option_id":"C","text":"Squaring gives the circle \\((x-4)^2+y^2=16\\), centre \\((4,0)\\), radius \\(4\\)."},{"option_id":"D","text":"Square both sides: \\(x^2+y^2=4\\big((x-3)^2+y^2\\big)\\iff(x-4)^2+y^2=4\\), the circle with centre \\((4,0)\\) and radius \\(2\\)."}]

question_text: Which is a factorisation of \(z^4+4\) into two quadratic factors with real coefficients?
